meta.title: mtmux changelog — every release, what shipped, what broke
meta.description: Every mtmux release: hosted pairing over a CPace PAKE, the sealed tunnel, QR sign-in, optional accounts, and the single-port CLI that started it.

hero.title: What shipped.
hero.lead: mtmux is young and the version number says so. Releases are listed here when they are on npm — nothing is dated before it exists.

entries.text: The routes that hand over files were the one way past the approval model. <cmd>GET /file</cmd> and <cmd>GET /recording</cmd> authenticated a token and then served bytes off the machine's disk without asking anybody — while the same token on the websocket put a question on the owner's screen. Both now cross the same gate.

Asking is the default everywhere, terminal or not. It used to depend on whether a terminal was attached, so a machine started by systemd or <cmd>nohup</cmd> trusted silently — the deployments least likely to be watched were the ones that quietly stopped asking. A headless machine can still be asked: <cmd>mtmux approve</cmd> in any other shell, or the app on a phone that is already connected.

<cmd>trust</cmd> no longer covers a device the machine has never recorded. It is a reconnect policy, and nothing about a stolen token is a reconnect. It waives the question for devices on your own list and nothing else.
Signing in with a token no longer throws that token away because nobody has approved the connection yet. Being slow to reach the laptop used to mean going and finding the token again.
A valid token is no longer permission. Approval is asked per connection — loopback, LAN and tunnelled alike — not once per credential, and nothing about the machine is sent before the answer.

One answer covers a device while it stays connected and for two minutes after its last socket closes, so tabs and a reconnect on a train are one act of connecting rather than a prompt every few minutes.
<cmd>x</cmd> in the live panel removes every device at once, in one question that names the count.
The panel says what the tunnel is doing — connecting, up, or down and retrying — instead of only whether it is up.
<cmd>--confirm-reconnect</cmd> and <cmd>--trust-reconnect</cmd> were parsed and then ignored; the stored policy decided every run whatever was typed.
A refusal no longer wipes a healthy pairing. The browser used to read any auth failure as “you have been forgotten” and send you back to pairing from scratch.
A spent code is replaced with a live QR rather than an offer to press a key nobody had been told about.
The live panel carries the code that is claimable right now, so it survives the banner scrolling away.
<cmd>mtmux devices remove</cmd>, which is what the panel’s <cmd>r</cmd> already called it. <cmd>revoke</cmd> stays as an alias.
Nothing the panel draws can be wider than the terminal. The approval screen’s answer line used to wrap off the bottom of a short one — the line telling you how to say no.
Two tabs of one browser are two rows again; both used to share a key, so every lookup matched the first.
A live local code is taken down when a tunnel opens, instead of staying claimable for 24 hours with nothing on screen showing it.
One key gets rid of a device and means it: the credential dies, the socket closes, and it must pair again.
A removed device loses its tunnel keys, not just its token.
A new code no longer reprints the whole banner, and the log stopped repeating what the panel already shows.
Six digits to type in local mode, so “I cannot scan that” has an answer short of copying a 64-character token.
Every path asks before it lets a device in — scanning the QR on your own wifi included. A network is not a person.
The device list is every device this machine trusts, not only the connected ones, with <cmd>e</cmd> to rename and <cmd>a</cmd> to flip whether a known device is asked about.
Press <cmd>t</cmd> in a running <cmd>mtmux start</cmd> to open the tunnel without restarting.
The local pairing code has a guess budget, and the endpoint has the same per-address backoff as token auth.
The offer is burned before the human is asked, not after — a correct code left live while a question sits on screen is a code an attacker can retry.
A live device panel in <cmd>mtmux start</cmd>: who is connected, what they may do, and the keys to act on them.
Recording with <cmd>mtmux record</cmd> — asciinema v2 casts on your own disk, shareable as their own scope.
Peer-supplied names are stripped at every terminal render site, not only at ingress.
Hosted pairing: <cmd>mtmux</cmd> opens a sealed tunnel and prints a QR and a pairing code, so a phone anywhere can attach without port forwarding.
The pairing handshake is a CPace PAKE over ristretto255. The broker routes on two digits and never receives the other four.
Sealed transport: HKDF-SHA256 key schedule, AES-256-GCM frames, per-direction nonces and a counter that rejects replays.
Device keys. A paired browser reconnects with a signed challenge, so the code is needed exactly once and <cmd>mtmux devices</cmd> can revoke it.
Optional accounts via OAuth device authorization — <cmd>mtmux login</cmd>, <cmd>whoami</cmd>, <cmd>servers</cmd> — plus multi-server and the Pro plan.
<cmd>mtmux doctor</cmd>, <cmd>status</cmd> and <cmd>stop</cmd>, and <cmd>--local</cmd> for a run that contacts no broker at all.
Binds the LAN by default when there is one, and prints a scannable sign-in code instead of asking you to copy a token.
Scoped session tokens and throttling on failed authentication in the relay.
Web and relay are served from one port, with dev and production behaving the same way.
Reconnect robustness, authenticated media requests, and sign-in via the URL fragment.
The file browser now opens at the directory the relay actually allows, rather than failing at the root.
The <cmd>mtmux</cmd> CLI itself: one npm package that bundles the web client and the relay into a single process on one port.
Security and resource-lifecycle hardening in the relay, and a clean error when the port is already in use.
Attach to a running tmux server from a browser: real panes, scrollback, and a modifier row built for a phone.
Session, window and pane management, a file browser, and a terminal view that survives reattaching.

subscribe: Releases are published to <ghLink>GitHub</ghLink> and to npm. <cmd>mtmux version</cmd> prints what you have installed; upgrading is <cmd>npm i -g mtmux</cmd> like any other package.
